## 2. Hierarchy body — every syllabus sub-point
### Biotechnological applications in medicine: insulin
### gene therapy
### therapeutic proteins

Fill order per concept: definition → structure → process → significance (§3.2). Step-by-step numbered points, Pioneer style.

Medical biotech manufactures what the body fails to make, or fixes the gene itself. **Recombinant insulin** (1982) replaced animal pancreas extract. **Gene therapy** attempts to deliver a working gene into a patient's cells — the classic case being ADA-SCID ('bubble boy' immune deficiency), treated with the ADA gene delivered in a disabled vector. **Therapeutic proteins** — growth hormone, clotting factors, interferon — are all made by cloned genes in fermenters.

**Concept flow — from protein replacement to gene repair (study in this order)**

| Step | Concept | Status |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Recombinant protein replacement | Mature, routine: insulin, hGH, factor VIII, interferon |
| 2 | Vaccines by cloning | Hepatitis B vaccine made from the cloned surface antigen gene in yeast |
| 3 | Gene therapy — somatic | Deliver a functional gene to the patient's cells (ADA-SCID, 1990); changes NOT inherited |
| 4 | Gene therapy — germline | Would change eggs/sperm — banned on ethical grounds |
| 5 | Personalised medicine | Genotype-based drug choice and dosing (pharmacogenomics) |

**Recombinant medical products — the master table**

| Product | Treats | Produced in |
|---|---|---|
| Human insulin (Humulin) | Diabetes mellitus | E. coli / yeast |
| Growth hormone (hGH) | Pituitary dwarfism | E. coli |
| Factor VIII | Haemophilia A | Mammalian cell culture |
| Interferon | Viral infections, some cancers | E. coli / yeast |
| Hepatitis B vaccine | Hepatitis B | Yeast (cloned HBsAg gene) |
| Erythropoietin (EPO) | Anaemia of kidney failure | Mammalian cells |

**Gene therapy — the ADA-SCID template**

| Stage | What happens | Note |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Diagnose the defect | ADA enzyme missing → toxic metabolites destroy T cells → severe combined immunodeficiency |
| 2 | Clone the normal ADA gene | Into a disabled retroviral vector |
| 3 | Harvest the patient's bone-marrow / lymphocyte cells | Ex vivo approach |
| 4 | Transduce the cells with the vector | Cells now carry the working gene |
| 5 | Reinfuse into the patient | First successful human gene therapy, 1990 (Ashanti DeSilva) |
| 6 | Limitations | Effects temporary (cells die); vector safety (immunoreaction); high cost; somatic only — not heritable |

## 6. Key terms and statements
Every new term defined once; exam-grade definitions live here and in keyPoints (block VI).

**Worked example — why ADA-SCID was the right first case.** The disease is caused by ONE known gene; the target cells (bone marrow/lymphocytes) can be removed, treated outside the body and reinfused; and even partial ADA restoration gives clear clinical benefit. Perfect first trial: single gene, accessible target, measurable outcome. Most diseases fail at least one of those three — which is why gene therapy has been slow to generalise despite this landmark success.

## 8. Summary and self-check
5–10 line chapter summary, self-check questions and the common-confusions list (block VIII) — completed in the unit fill pass.

**Summary.** Medicine runs on cloned genes at two levels: manufacture the missing protein (insulin, factor VIII) or deliver the missing gene (ADA-SCID). The first is routine; the second remains limited by vector safety and transience. **Self-check:** can you list the five steps of the ex vivo gene therapy protocol?

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Human insulin: two-chain A (21 aa) + B (30 aa) linked by disulphide; proinsulin → C-peptide removed; engineered in E. coli since 1983 — the chain numbers are the marks.
Trick 2: Gene therapy: ADA deficiency — lymphocytes from the patient, functional ADA gene inserted by retrovirus, cells returned (ex vivo); marrow transplant as alternative.
Trick 3: Other products: hGH, interferon, blood clotting factor VIII, vaccines (Hepatitis B surface antigen in yeast) — the product bank.
Trick 4: Molecular diagnosis: ELISA (antigen–antibody), PCR (pathogen/mutation detection) — the two diagnostic tools.
